evidence_set: Qualifications: no measurement before the drug night (day 1 was tested during intoxication), volunteers recruited by snowballing at one club, intake unverified, 7 of the 12 in the ecstasy group also drank, and no simple-effect test for day 5. evidence_set: The authors are reasonably certain the men took phencyclidine from their history of street drugs often found to contain it and from the clinical picture; no laboratory confirmation is reported. As cited from earlier literature, PCP's analgesia usually lasts 1 to 3 hours and its psychotomimetic effects 18 to 24 hours; prolonged reactions had been reported in 1 of 65 surgical patients (10 days) and in four people with chronic schizophrenia (more than 4 weeks). The authors do not know why their patients were ill for 2 to 4 weeks and list dose, slow metabolism, toxic metabolites, idiosyncrasy or precipitation or exacerbation of a schizophrenic process.

evidence_set: Predicted time for impairment to fall to g = -0.25 at the reference dose in other use, smoked / vaporised / oral, in minutes: aggregate 300 / 350 / 480; divided attention 383 / 428 / not calculable (oral peak predicted less impairing than g = -0.25); tracking 386 / 430 / 573; information processing 486 / 530 / 557; reaction time 232 / 276 / 492; working memory 277 / 321 / not calculable (oral peak predicted less impairing than g = -0.25); lane weaving (SDLP) 427 / 472 / not calculable; conflict control under 60 smoked, 71 vaporised and 665 oral; sustained attention under 60 inhaled. No intervals are given.

The abstract says most driving-related cognitive skills would recover within about 5 h and almost all within about 7 h of inhaling the reference dose; in Table 9, information processing (486 and 530 min, smoked and vaporised) and lane weaving (SDLP, a driving measure: 427 and 472 min) take longer than 7 h. Limitations named by the authors: the models assume a fixed rate of recovery, few studies tested people who use cannabis regularly or longer intervals (4-6 h), doses were absolute rather than per body weight, and women were underrepresented. The recovery threshold (g = -0.25) is the authors' own definition of no meaningful impact.

evidence_set: Stages: N1 0.15 (-0.07 to 0.37); N2 0.01 (-0.21 to 0.23); slow-wave sleep 0.14 (-0.07 to 0.35); REM -0.04 (-0.52 to 0.45), I-squared 77.5%, with both arms of one dronabinol trial in sleep apnea raising REM (1.16 and 0.72) and CBD in REM behaviour disorder lowering it (-0.98); REM latency -0.03 (-0.56 to 0.50), I-squared 76.1%. Of 14 administration studies, six found less REM sleep and one more.

The six pooled administration studies were all oral: THC with or without CBD in 8 healthy volunteers, dronabinol in sleep apnea (15 and 73 people), CBD in 26 healthy volunteers and in people with REM behaviour disorder and Parkinson's disease (17 and 16 in two arms), and a THC, CBN and CBD product in 23 people with insomnia. Early 1972-1982 studies (2 to 11 people, mostly high THC doses) lacked data for pooling; most reported less REM sleep. The authors note the clinical literature almost exclusively studies oral use, not inhalation.

evidence_set: Across all seven withdrawal studies: total sleep time fell in three and did not change in four; time to fall asleep rose in five; waking after sleep onset rose in three; REM rose in three. For the three pooled withdrawal studies, the data used came from the first three days in two and from days four to six in one.

Pooled withdrawal studies: Feinberg et al. 1975 (n = 7) and 1976 (n = 11), placebo substituted for daily high oral THC doses in experienced men, rated high risk of bias; Vandrey et al. 2011 (n = 20), sleep before and during abstinence in people actively using cannabis, aware they had stopped, rated low. The authors cite a suggestion (Bolla et al. 2010) that the REM rebound in these studies may be accentuated by their very high oral THC doses.
